summary: Emmanuel Turlay, CEO of Sematic and creator of AirTrain, tackles the problem of evaluating language models for specific use cases—a challenge unique to LLMs because they generate unstructured text rather than structured outputs like numbers, classes, or bounding boxes. In traditional supervised ML, well-established metrics exist: RMSE and MAE for regressions, precision/recall/F1 for classifiers, and intersection-over-union for computer vision. For LLMs, metrics like BLEU (precision-based n-gram overlap, useful for translation) and ROUGE (recall-based, useful for summarization) exist but don't account for intelligibility or grammatical correctness. Without labeled references, metrics like density and coverage measure how summaries relate to source text. However, these only apply to high-level tasks such as translation and summarization. Standardized benchmarks—GLUE (9 language understanding tasks including paraphrase detection and sentiment analysis), HellaSwag (natural language inference and common sense), TriviaQA (almost a million trivia questions), and ARC (high school science reasoning)—help compare models broadly but don't indicate performance on specific tasks like extracting symptoms from doctor's notes, recipe ingredients, or forming API query payloads. Turlay's key solution is the LLM-as-judge approach: use another model to grade outputs by describing the task, grading criteria, and a numerical scale in a scoring prompt. The grading model generates a score, enabling distribution analysis across a dataset. An example scores politeness of email closing words from 1 to 10. GPT-4 is the best grader but costly; Flan T5 offers a good speed-correctness trade-off. AirTrain operationalizes this: upload datasets, select models (Llama 2, Falcon, Flan T5, or custom), describe properties to measure, and visualize metric distributions for data-driven model selection.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Problem Statement
sections.summary: Emmanuel introduces himself as CEO of Sematic, the company behind AirTrain. He frames evaluation as a difficult problem in the language modeling space: unlike other ML areas, there is no straightforward, one-size-fits-all process to evaluate LLMs for a specific use case.

sections.title: What Is Model Evaluation and Traditional ML Metrics
sections.summary: Model evaluation is the statistical measurement of model performance on a large dataset independent from training data. It comes after training or fine-tuning and is compared to running test suites in CI. Traditional supervised ML has well-defined metrics: RMSE and MAE for regressions, precision/recall/F1 for classifiers, and intersection-over-union for computer vision.

sections.title: LLM-Specific Text Metrics
sections.summary: LLMs generate unstructured text, so inferences differing from ground truth aren't necessarily wrong. BLEU measures precision-based n-gram overlap (useful for translation and summarization) but ignores intelligibility and grammatical correctness. ROUGE measures recall of token sequences (useful for summarization). Without labeled references, density and coverage quantify summary representativeness and derivativeness. These metrics only apply to high-level tasks.

sections.title: Benchmarks and Their Limitations
sections.summary: Standardized benchmarks rank models: GLUE tests language understanding across 9 tasks, HellaSwag tests natural language inference and common sense, TriviaQA tests knowledge with ~1M trivia questions, and ARC tests science reasoning. These metrics and benchmarks help draw a landscape of model comparisons but don't tell you how a model performs on your particular task or input data type.

sections.title: LLM-as-Judge Approach
sections.summary: Turlay proposes using another model to grade LLM outputs: describe the task and grading criteria in a scoring prompt with a numerical scale, then have a grading model score the inferences. Example: scoring politeness of email closings from 1 to 10. GPT-4 is the best grader but costly; Flan T5 offers a good speed-correctness trade-off.

sections.title: AirTrain Tool
sections.summary: AirTrain operationalizes the LLM-as-judge approach: upload a dataset, select models to compare (Llama 2, Falcon, Flan T5, or custom models), describe properties to measure, and visualize metric distributions across the dataset. Users can sign up for early access to make data-driven decisions about LLM choice.

demonstrations: Scoring politeness of email closing words from 1 to 10 using an LLM judge ('please let us know as your earliest convenience' scores highly; 'tell me ASAP' scores poorly)
AirTrain workflow: upload dataset, select models to compare, describe properties to measure, visualize metric distributions across the dataset
limitations: BLEU does not account for intelligibility or grammatical correctness
Existing LLM metrics only apply to high-level tasks like translation and summarization
Benchmarks don't indicate performance on specific applications such as extracting symptoms from doctor's notes, recipe ingredients, or forming API payloads
GPT-4 as a grader is costly for large datasets
No one-size-fits-all process exists for evaluating LLMs on specific use cases
